answer:
**Stereo depth comes from how much the same point shifts between two camera views.** For rectified cameras, corresponding points lie on the same image row. A nearby point shifts more horizontally than a distant point. That horizontal difference is disparity. [1](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html)

With focal length f in pixels, baseline B in meters, and disparity d in pixels, depth is $Z=fB/d$. If f=800 pixels, B=0.1 m, and d=40 pixels, depth is 2 m. If disparity falls to 4 pixels, depth becomes 20 m.

**The same pixel error becomes much worse far away.** Differentiating gives $|dZ/dd|=fB/d^2$. A one-pixel disparity uncertainty is about 0.05 m at d=40 but about 5 m at d=4 under the local approximation. The far-range estimate can therefore look numerically precise while being physically very uncertain.

A larger baseline increases disparity for the same depth and improves sensitivity, but also increases viewpoint differences and occlusions, making correspondence harder. Textureless surfaces, reflections, and calibration errors cause additional failures beyond the derivative calculation. Keep focal length and disparity in consistent pixel units, especially after resizing images. Report depth confidence and reject unreliable matches instead of treating every computed disparity as equally trustworthy.

**Technical details and references.**

For rectified pinhole cameras with parallel image planes, $x_L=fX/Z$ and $x_R=f(X-B)/Z$. Subtracting gives disparity $d=fB/Z$, hence depth $Z=fB/d$. Use consistent units: if disparity is in pixels, focal length must be in pixels. [1](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html)

$$\left|\frac{dZ}{dd}\right|=\frac{fB}{d^2}=\frac{Z^2}{fB},\quad \sigma_Z\approx\frac{Z^2}{fB}\sigma_d.$$

Far objects have small disparity, so a fixed pixel error creates rapidly growing depth uncertainty. Calibration error, occlusion, textureless regions, and correspondence mistakes add errors beyond this local approximation. Larger baseline improves depth sensitivity but increases occlusions and matching difficulty. Report uncertainty rather than treating every disparity as equally reliable.
